name: Lena Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Lena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior stockperson at Kerrow Farm, run by the Pennington family firm. They've got sixteen thousand free-range laying hens in four sheds, plus wheat and oilseed rape on the rest of the land. I'm in at six, walking the sheds, checking water, feed and dead birds, then I'm on the egg packing line most of the morning. Afternoons it's cleaning, letting the hens out onto the range, and learning the grading machine, which I'm still bad at.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a school cook for fifteen years. I cooked for four hundred children a day, so sixteen thousand hens don't frighten me, but the egg grader still does. When my dad died four years ago I wanted a change, and Mrs Pennington from church offered me a start. They pay well because they can't keep staff.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mark, my husband, sells tractors and farm machinery at the dealership in town, on commission. Josh is sixteen and desperate to farm, Ellie's twelve. We've a mortgage, and Dad left me enough that we've well over a year of savings. I use AI now and then, Mark showed me, mostly for meal plans and the odd letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world's got enough to worry about. I'd say at church that people should spend less time on their phones and more time with each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it means steady. My job's fine, Mark's selling, the savings are there. The thing on my mind is Josh, who wants to go to agricultural college, and whether farming is a sensible thing to send a boy into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Kerrow and finally get confident on the grader. I'd help Josh apply for the agricultural college for next September, and keep the savings for his course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit of mum worry, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about Josh farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's hard and the money's thin unless you own land, which we don't. I'd rather he did it with his eyes open. Mark says let the boy try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's hard about the grader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The egg grader is all screens and error codes. When the grader jams, I'm stood there and Kev has to come and reset it. I'll get there.

say: The world has **enough to worry** about already.
People should spend **less time on phones** and more with each other.
think: Life stays **steady**: her job, Mark's sales and the savings are fine.
Her real question is whether **farming suits Josh**.
do: **Get confident** on the egg grading machine.
**Help** Josh apply to agricultural college for next September.

fieldNote: Came to farming after **her father died**, through a church contact.
Savings from **inheritance** make the household secure.
Her focus is her son's **farming future**, not her own job.

steps.text: Practise on the Kerrow egg grader until she can reset it alone
Help Josh apply to agricultural college for next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hands-on work is safer, and that's why trades and farming matter. I'd say it to the other mums at the school gate who push their kids into office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is Mark, not me. My husband Mark sells tractors for a living, and the first thing AI learns is how to write a quote. Farmers would order online, with a computer doing the advice, and his commission shrinks. Mark says he'd sell the robots instead, and maybe he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside each month in case Mark's commission drops. Once the Penningtons' new egg software was settled, I'd learn it properly, not just watch Kev. And I'd keep Josh on track for college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Watchful about Mark's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Mark say when you raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark laughed and said farmers like a handshake, not a chatbot. But he's had two big orders go online already this year. He didn't laugh as long as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about Josh's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd want him on a course that includes the machines, though, not just animals.

She'd tell **school-gate mums** not to push kids into office jobs.
think: Her worry is **Mark's commission**, as AI writes quotes and advice.
Mark thinks he could **sell robots** instead, and he might be right.
do: **Save** a bit more each month in case Mark's pay drops.
**Learn** the Penningtons' egg software once it's settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to stick together and help each other through it. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not handouts. And at church I'd ask for prayers for every family in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the worst one for us. If my husband Mark loses the dealership job in 2028 and I lose the hens in 2031, our savings become a countdown. Egg sheds are already half machines, the robots would finish the job. I'd be lying awake working out how many months we'd last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut the extras, no holiday, cancel the kitchen we were planning. I'd talk Josh out of agricultural college and into an engineering apprenticeship. And I'd ask at the care home where the chapel volunteers whether they'd train me as a carer, because people want people when they're old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I'd be keeping it from the kids, but not from Mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would the savings last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year and a half if we both lost everything, maybe two with the cuts. The mortgage has eleven years left. That's the number I'd keep doing in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Josh take the change of plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. He'd slam his door. But I'd tell him he can still work on farms, fixing the machines, and that's more use than one more pair of hands.

fieldNote: **Two earners** exposed: Mark's thinking work first, her egg work three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so plan. Families that start now will be fine. I'd tell the women at church to sit down with their husbands and write it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to steer our son Josh towards fixing the robots instead of doing the work they replace. Mark has until 2031 to move into servicing or something. My hens go in 2034, I'd be fifty-one. It's still two jobs, just not at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder for the next few years and keep the kitchen on hold. I'd do the carer training part-time from 2029, so I'm ready. Josh would do the farm course with an engineering add-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd sleep most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mark move into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark talked about the servicing side at the dealership, the mechanics. He'd hate the pay cut. But it's a job with his hands, and his dad was a mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still the farm course for Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years gives him time to try it. If the machines are the future, he'll learn them there too.

Couples should sit down together and **write it out**.

fieldNote: The **staggered timing** of the two job losses is what eases her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and families that waste it have only themselves to blame. I'd say it kindly, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather my son Josh spent ten years learning to mend machines than ten years learning a job that disappears. For me and Mark, 2036 hits his sales and 2039 my hens, when I'm fifty-six. We'd have the mortgage nearly paid. It's on my mind but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Kerrow. Keep saving at the usual rate. Get Josh into an apprenticeship that covers the robots, and nudge Mark towards servicing over the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie wants to be a nurse, and I'd say good, people will always need people. I'd tell her the same as Josh: learn the machines too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your view on AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them more, I think, once everyone else does. I'm not against them. I just like to see they work first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us get hit within three years. What would help is good apprenticeships for grown-ups and for kids, paid properly, and employers like the Penningtons keeping people on to work with the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About couples. A family can ride out one lost job, but two at once is how you lose the house.

headlineQuote: A family can ride out one lost job, but two at once is how you lose the house.
